rationale: Zechariah says foreigners will dwell in Azotus while their arrogance is brought down. Amos announces destruction of inhabitants from Azotus. The shared city and its population provide the connection; the outcomes are not presented as identical.
source_text: Foreigners will dwell in Azotus, and I will bring down the foreigners’ arrogance.

target_units.text: I will destroy inhabitants from Azotus, and a tribe will be removed from Ascalon. I will bring My hand against Accaron, and the remaining foreigners will perish,” says the Lord.

relationship: historical context for the comparison with the Jebusite
rationale: Zechariah compares Akkaron with the Jebusite within an announcement about remaining for God and belonging alongside Judah. Joshua records Jebusites continuing to live in Jerusalem when Judah could not destroy them. This supplies a concrete account of the named people remaining in Judah's setting, without identifying Akkaron with Jerusalem.
source_text: I will remove their blood from their mouth and their detestable things from between their teeth. This one too will remain for our God; they will be like a commander of a thousand in Judah, and Akkaron like the Jebusite.

target_units.text: The Jebusites lived in Jerusalem, and the sons of Judah could not destroy them. The Jebusites lived in Jerusalem until that day.

relationship: the protected holy city no longer traversed by outsiders
rationale: Zechariah promises the Lord's stand for His house, preventing passage and renewed expulsion. Joel likewise names His dwelling in Zion and says foreigners will no longer pass through holy Jerusalem. Both connect divine presence with protection of that sacred place.
source_text: I will take a stand for My house to prevent passing through or returning. No one driving them out will come upon them again, for now I have seen with My own eyes.

target_units.text: You will recognize that I am the Lord your God, dwelling in Zion on My holy mountain. Jerusalem will be a holy city, and foreigners will no longer pass through her.

relationship: explicit later prophetic quotation applied to Jesus' entry
rationale: Zechariah announces Zion's gentle king mounted on a beast of burden and young colt. Matthew explicitly introduces a fulfilled prophetic saying about Zion's meek king riding a donkey and colt, then narrates the disciples bringing them to Jesus. The named address, king and mounts establish the quotation relationship.
source_text: Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion; proclaim, daughter Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes to you, righteous and saving, gentle, and mounted upon a beast of burden and a young colt.

target_units.text: This happened so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled:
“Tell the daughter of Zion: ‘Behold, your King comes to you, meek and mounted upon a donkey, and upon a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.’”
The disciples went and did as Jesus directed them.
They brought the donkey and the colt, placed the garments upon them, and He sat upon them.

relationship: explicit written saying about Zion's king on a colt
rationale: John introduces Jesus' sitting on a young donkey with a written saying addressing daughter Zion and announcing her king on a donkey's colt. Those elements correspond to Zechariah's announcement. John preserves its own introductory command not to fear rather than Zechariah's call to rejoice.
source_text: Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion; proclaim, daughter Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes to you, righteous and saving, gentle, and mounted upon a beast of burden and a young colt.

target_units.text: Jesus found a young donkey and sat upon it, just as it is written,
“Do not fear, daughter Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting upon a donkey’s colt.”
His disciples did not understand these things at first. But when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things were written about Him and that they had done these things to Him.

relationship: royal peace and dominion extending to seas and rivers
rationale: Zechariah's coming king is associated with destroyed battle weapons, abundant peace and rule reaching waters and river outlets. The royal psalm likewise combines abundant peace with rule from sea to sea and from the river to the world's ends. The expansive rule and peace connect them without making their geographical wording identical.
source_text: He will destroy chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem; the battle bow will be destroyed, and abundance and peace from the nations. He will rule waters as far as the sea and the earth’s river outlets.

target_units.text: Righteousness will arise in his days, and abundant peace until the moon is taken away.
And he will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the inhabited world.

rationale: Zechariah attributes the release of prisoners from a waterless pit to covenant blood. Exodus describes Moses sprinkling blood and identifying it as the blood of the covenant the Lord made with the people. The covenant-blood expression is shared, while prisoner release belongs to Zechariah's statement.
source_text: You, by covenant blood, released your prisoners from a pit with no water.

target_units.text: Moses took half the blood and poured it into bowls; the other half he poured against the altar.
He took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people. They said, “We will do and obey everything the Lord has spoken.”
Moses took the blood and sprinkled it over the people, saying, “Behold, the blood of the covenant the Lord has made with you concerning all these words.”

relationship: captivity pictured through a pit containing no water
rationale: Zechariah speaks of prisoners released from a pit with no water. Genesis describes Joseph seized by his brothers and thrown into an empty pit expressly said to have no water. The particular waterless confinement image connects the passages, without identifying the prisoners as Joseph.
source_text: You, by covenant blood, released your prisoners from a pit with no water.

target_units.text: And when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped Joseph of the tunic of many colours which was upon him.
And they took him and cast him into the pit; and the pit was empty, having no water.

relationship: Zion divinely equipped to overcome hostile nations
rationale: Zechariah pictures Judah as the Lord's bent bow and Zion's children handled like a fighter's sword against Greek children. Micah likewise gives daughter Zion iron horns and bronze hooves to thresh hostile nations. Both turn God's people into an image of an empowered instrument against opponents, with different weapons and named enemies.
source_text: For I bent you, Judah, as a bow for Myself; I filled Ephraim, and I will rouse your children, Zion, against the Greeks’ children and handle you like a fighter’s sword.

target_units.text: Now many nations have gathered against you, saying, “We will rejoice over her, and our eyes will look upon Zion!”
But they did not know the Lord’s thought or understand His counsel, for He gathered them like sheaves of a threshing floor.

Rise and thresh them, daughter of Zion, for I will make your horns iron and your hooves bronze. With them you will melt down nations and grind many peoples fine; you will dedicate their multitude to the Lord and their strength to the Lord of all the earth.

relationship: the Lord's warfare pictured through missiles and lightning
rationale: Zechariah describes the Lord above His people, a missile going like lightning and His threatening trumpet. The psalm likewise depicts His heavenly voice, arrows and lightning throwing enemies into turmoil. Both combine divine intervention with missile and lightning imagery, while the trumpet is particular to Zechariah here.
source_text: The Lord will be over them; a missile will go out like lightning. The Lord Almighty will sound a trumpet and go in the tumult of His threat.

target_units.text: And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave His voice.
And He sent out arrows and scattered them; He multiplied lightning flashes and threw them into turmoil.

relationship: the Lord explicitly shielding His people
rationale: Zechariah announces that the Lord Almighty will shield the people in battle. Isaiah likewise says the Lord will shield Jerusalem, rescue, preserve and save. The stated protective action connects the promises without importing Zechariah's wine and altar images into Isaiah.
source_text: The Lord Almighty will shield them. They will consume them, bury them with sling stones and drink them down like wine; they will fill the altar like bowls.

target_units.text: Like flying birds, so the Lord will shield Jerusalem, rescue, preserve and save.”

relationship: the Lord saves and tends His people as sheep
rationale: Zechariah says the Lord will save His people like sheep. Ezekiel likewise promises the Lord's personal search, gathering, feeding and care for His sheep. Both expressly describe divine preservation through the flock image.
source_text: The Lord will save them on that day, His people like sheep, because holy stones roll over His land.

target_units.text: For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will seek out My sheep and visit them.

As a shepherd seeks his flock on a day when there is gloom and cloud among separated sheep, so I will seek out My sheep and drive them away from every place where they scattered on a day of cloud and gloom.

I will bring them out from the nations, gather them from the countries and bring them into their own land. I will feed them upon Israel’s mountains, in the ravines and in every dwelling place of the land.
I will feed them in good pasture, and their folds will be upon Israel’s high mountain. There they will lie down, there rest in good delight, and graze in rich pasture upon Israel’s mountains.
I Myself will feed My sheep and give them rest, and they will know that I am the Lord. Thus says the Lord, the Lord:
I will seek the lost, bring back the wandering, bind up the broken, strengthen the failing and guard the strong. I will feed them with judgment.

relationship: grain and wine given with renewed favor toward the people
rationale: Zechariah names grain for young men and fragrant wine for virgins within the account of the people's salvation. Joel likewise follows the Lord's sparing of His people with a promise of grain, wine and oil. Both connect renewed provision with restored divine favor.
source_text: For whatever is good of him and whatever is beautiful from him: grain for young men and fragrant wine for virgins.

target_units.text: Then the Lord became jealous for His land and spared His people.
The Lord answered His people: “Look, I am sending out to you grain, wine and oil, and you will be filled with them. I will no longer give you over to reproach among the nations,
